analysis.one_liner: Ends the special antitrust-law exemptions enjoyed by freight railroads.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill by voice vote, but it sat on the House calendar and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Freight railroads are largely exempt from federal antitrust laws, the laws used to police price-fixing, monopolies, and anticompetitive mergers. This bill would remove those exemptions, letting the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, and private shippers sue railroads under the same antitrust rules that apply to nearly every other industry. It would also require the board that regulates railroads to consider the impact of rate agreements on shippers, consumers, and communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that ship goods by rail — grain farmers, coal-burning utilities, chemical and manufacturing companies — especially 'captive' shippers served by only one railroad, who pay some of the highest freight rates in the world. Their savings could eventually show up in lower prices for food, electricity, and manufactured goods.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the railroad exemptions from the antitrust laws, including for mergers, acquisitions, and ratemaking agreements, placing railroads under the same competition rules as other industries [S3] [S4].
Lets the Federal Trade Commission pursue rail carriers for unfair methods of competition and restores private parties' ability to seek court injunctions against railroad antitrust violations [S3].

Applies the antitrust laws to railroads regardless of whether the carrier has filed a rate with the regulator, removing a defense railroads have used to shield their rates from antitrust review [S3] [S4].
Requires the Surface Transportation Board, when reviewing rate agreements and transactions, to consider and document the impact on shippers, consumers, and affected communities [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads, which would face antitrust lawsuits from the government and from shippers, lose their freedom to set rates without competition-law review, and face antitrust scrutiny of future mergers.

drawbacks.text: The railroads' core objection: antitrust suits over rates could duplicate or conflict with the Surface Transportation Board's own regulatory scheme over rail rates, creating costly, parallel litigation and uncertainty for a capital-intensive industry [S2].

The bill grandfathers past deals: it bars lawsuits to dissolve or undo any merger or acquisition completed before enactment under an old exemption, so it could not unwind the consolidation that already shrank the number of major railroads [S4].
Litigation risk would fall partly on the shipping side too: private antitrust suits are expensive, and smaller shippers might still be outgunned by the railroads in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted fix: it puts railroads under the same antitrust rules as virtually every other industry and adds transparency requirements for rate agreements. Its main weakness is that it cannot undo the past — the wave of mergers that consolidated the industry into a handful of giants remains untouched — so its benefits would arrive mainly through future conduct, pricing, and merger review. The industry's concern about overlapping regulation is legitimate but not unusual; other regulated industries live under both antitrust law and a sector regulator.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it by voice vote in September 2009, but it was not formally reported to the floor until the last week of November 2010, when it was placed on the House calendar — and the Congress ended weeks later without anyone ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 7, 2009 by Rep. Tammy Baldwin with 21 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans, and referred to both the Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees [S1] [S5].

The Railroads subcommittee held a hearing in May 2009 and forwarded the bill to the full Judiciary Committee by voice vote in July 2009; the full committee ordered it reported, amended, by voice vote on September 16, 2009 [S6].

The committee's formal report came only on November 30, 2010, nearly fourteen months later, when the Transportation Committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the queue of bills awaiting a floor vote [S3] [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large freight railroads are better off: they kept their antitrust exemptions, their freedom to set rates and approve agreements without competition-law review, and their immunity from private antitrust suits — with no vote ever taken on the bill.

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 21 cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 21 of 435 House cosponsors (18 of 253 House Democrats, 3 of 178 House Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 18 Democrats and 3 Republicans.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and ordered it reported, amended, by voice vote in September 2009; formally reported it November 30, 2010.

for.name: Rail shippers (farm, coal, chemical, and manufacturing freight customers)
for.what_they_did: Supported restoring antitrust coverage for railroads, an issue they had pressed for years over rising freight rates.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote; it sat on the Union Calendar from November 30, 2010 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Class I freight railroads (Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern, Kansas City Southern)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and lobbied to preserve the industry's antitrust exemptions and Surface Transportation Board oversight.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 21 cosponsors were 18 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and the Judiciary Committee reported it by voice vote, but no roll-call vote was ever taken on the bill, and the freight railroads' opposition ran through both parties' fundraising and lobbying networks.

industries.note: The bill would end their exemptions from the antitrust laws, exposing their rates, rate agreements, and future mergers to antitrust suits by the government, the FTC, and private shippers. Their existing pricing power — especially over captive shippers with no alternative railroad — comes directly at the expense of the businesses and consumers paying freight-inflated prices.
These businesses would gain the right to sue railroads under antitrust law and challenge anticompetitive rate agreements, and their freight savings would eventually pass through to consumer prices.
Ending the railroad exemptions would open a new field of antitrust litigation against a major industry, generating work for competition lawyers and experts on both sides.
